title: Are Humans Really the Ultimate Super-Predator?
hook: Wild animals don't fear all humans equally — a 30-year review shows their alarm depends heavily on what kind of human they're facing.
key_points: Humans are often called the planet's "super-predator," but wild animals don't treat every human encounter the same way.
A review of three decades of research found animals become sharply more alert and feed less around people who pose a real lethal threat, like hunters or fishers.
Tourists, researchers, and other non-lethal humans trigger much weaker and less predictable reactions.
This suggests animals can distinguish between different kinds of human presence, not just react to "humans" as one uniform threat category.
content_html: Humans are often labeled the planet's ultimate "super-predator" — but a new review of three decades of research suggests wild animals aren't so easily fooled by that label.
extra_html: Analyzing decades of studies on how wildlife responds to human presence, researchers found that animals become much more alert and spend noticeably less time feeding when they encounter humans who pose a genuine lethal threat, such as hunters or fishers. Tourists, scientists, and other non-lethal visitors, by contrast, trigger far weaker and less predictable responses. The pattern suggests wild animals aren't simply reacting to "humans" as one uniform threat category — they appear to be reading context and adjusting their fear accordingly, much as they might with different predator species.

related.title: Mountain Lions Reshaped a Tiny Suburban Preserve
related.hook: When mountain lions started visiting a small preserve near San Francisco, deer backed off, plants recovered, and smaller predators shifted — trophic cascades aren't just for remote wilderness.

related.title: Keystone Species
related.hook: Some species pull more than their weight. Remove them, and an entire ecosystem can unravel — even when they were never the most abundant thing around.

flashcards.prompt: Do wild animals react the same way to every human they encounter?
flashcards.back_html: No — reactions depend heavily on context: hunters and fishers trigger sharp alertness, while tourists and researchers trigger much weaker, less predictable responses.

flashcards.prompt: What behavior change did animals show around humans posing a genuine lethal threat?

choices.text: They became much more alert and spent less time feeding
They showed no measurable behavior change at all
They approached those humans more closely than usual

flashcards.explanation_html: Across three decades of studies, lethal-threat encounters like hunting or fishing consistently raised alertness and cut into feeding time.

flashcards.prompt: What does this pattern suggest about how animals perceive humans?
flashcards.back_html: That they distinguish between different kinds of human presence and adjust their fear accordingly, rather than treating all humans as one uniform threat.
